newsitem.title: USA: Lands' End says demand lower on UPS strike.
newsitem.headline: Lands' End says demand lower on UPS strike.

text.p: Catalog company Lands' End Inc said Thursday it has received fewer customer calls since the United Parcel Service strike began, but orders still are being filled rapidly despite the setback.
The company said it has been shipping goods through the U.S. Postal Service's priority mail system, and most packages have been arriving to customers' homes in three to five days.

"Things are going remarkably well, all things considered. We've been able to ship all packages out of Dodgeville within one business day, which is our normal service standard," president and chief executive Michael Smith said in a statement.

"While we've seen a decline in the number of customer calls since the strike against UPS began, we want to assure our customers that everything is running smoothly in filling and shipping their orders," he said.
Earlier Lands' End said earnings rose 16.2 percent to $3.4 million, or $0.11 a share, in the second quarter. Sales rose 12.1 percent to $219.9 million.

The growth in sales during the quarter just ended came from specialty businesses and foreign-based operations and the core U.S. business, represented by the monthly and prospecting catalogs. The sales increase also reflected an overall rise in the number of catalogs and pages mailed.
Productivity, or sales per page, fell, partially due to the increase in pages mailed. Liquidations of excess inventory were about 6 percent of net sales in the quarter versus 8 percent a year ago.

Selling, general and administrative expenses rose 14.5 percent to $96.8 million versus the second quarter of 1996. As a percentage of sales, SG&A was 44.0 percent, compared with 43.1 percent in the same period last year. The increase was due to relatively higher order-fulfillment expenses due to higher wages and a higher level of backorders, additional investment in information systems and relatively higher costs due to increased catalog circulation. The company increased the number of catalogs and pages mailed to customers, but paper prices were lower than in the prior year.
